title: The Bone Beds and the Frontier: Darwin in Argentina, Patagonia and Tierra del Fuego
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: The Mount, and the Road to Plymouth

stops.name: The Mount, Shrewsbury: the birth
stops.date_confidence: attested; the coordinate is corrected from the pool's 52.7069 / -2.7554, which is Shrewsbury town centre and about 900 m off the house
stops.campa: In the brick house above the Severn that the family calls The Mount, Susannah Wedgwood bears a fifth child to the physician Robert Darwin, and they name him Charles Robert. Money comes into the house from two directions, pottery on the mother's side, medicine and land on the father's. His grandfather Erasmus Darwin, seven years dead, has already put into verse the notion that all warm-blooded life descends from a single living filament; the family reads that as an eccentric's poem and not as a program. The boy collects beetles, minerals and birds' eggs, and is told by his father that he cares for nothing but shooting, dogs and rat-catching.
suggested_refs: The Mount, Shrewsbury, the Darwin family house above the Severn

stops.name: University of Edinburgh, Old College: the medicine he cannot stomach
stops.date_confidence: the two sessions 1825 to 1827 are attested; the month is set to the opening of the Edinburgh session and is inferred
stops.campa: Sent north at sixteen to read medicine as his father and grandfather had, he finds the lectures dull and the operating theatre unbearable, and twice walks out of surgery performed on a child without anaesthetic, there being none. What he keeps from Edinburgh is off the syllabus. He learns to skin and mount specimens, and he dredges the Firth of Forth for marine invertebrates with Robert Grant, who opens sea mats and sponges under a lens and talks, without lowering his voice, about the transmutation of species. Darwin takes the method away with him and leaves the doctrine where he found it.
suggested_refs: Robert Grant's Firth of Forth dredging work on marine invertebrates

stops.name: Christ's College, Cambridge: Henslow, and a book about the equinoctial regions
stops.date_confidence: the residence 1828 to 1831 is attested; month and day are unknown and default to 01
stops.campa: He is moved to Cambridge to be made a clergyman, reads for an ordinary degree, and spends his real attention on beetles. The botanist John Stevens Henslow walks him out into the fens, teaches him to look at a plant as evidence rather than as ornament, and is the man who will later put his name forward for a berth. In the same rooms he reads Alexander von Humboldt's Personal Narrative of travel in the equinoctial regions, and copies passages out to read aloud to friends. He says long afterwards that the book stirred up in him a burning zeal to add even a humble contribution to natural science.
suggested_refs: Humboldt's Personal Narrative, the book Darwin credits with sending him to sea

stops.name: Plymouth Sound: HMS Beagle sails
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: After two false starts against the weather the Beagle puts out from Plymouth on the twenty-seventh of December, a ten-gun brig of two hundred and forty tons carrying seventy-four people, a collection of chronometers, and three Fuegians being taken home. Robert FitzRoy commands. Darwin is twenty-two, holds no official post, draws no salary, pays his own way, and is aboard in large part so that the captain will have someone of his own class to eat with. The survey is meant to run two years. It runs five, and he is seasick for most of them.
suggested_refs: The Beagle's rerigged decks and chronometer room, refitted at Devonport for the second survey
sources: Darwin, Journal of Researches, 2nd ed. (1845), Ch. I

stops.name: Porto Praya, Cape Verde: a white band in the cliff
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The first tropical ground under his feet is volcanic and nearly bare. Walking the sea cliffs of Santiago he finds a horizontal white band running through the black rock high above the water, and picks out of it the shells of creatures still living in the bay below. Lava has flowed over an old sea bed, and the whole mass has since been lifted clear of the water. He is carrying the first volume of Lyell, lent to him by FitzRoy, and here he begins reading a landscape as a record of slow movement rather than of ruin. Humboldt is the reason he is examining a cliff at all.
suggested_refs: The raised shell band in the sea cliffs of Santiago, Darwin's first geological observation of the voyage
sources: Darwin, Journal of Researches, 2nd ed. (1845), Ch. I

stops.name: Salvador da Bahia: the first Brazilian forest
stops.date_confidence: contested: the chronology lens and the Beagle voyage article give 28 February 1832, the geography lens gives 29 February; the earlier date is used and the conflict is not resolved
stops.campa: The Beagle anchors off Bahia and Darwin walks alone into the forest behind the town. Nothing in his reading has prepared him for the noise of it, or for the number of kinds of thing living at once inside a single acre. He writes that his mind is a chaos of delight. In the same weeks he watches slavery worked in a Brazilian port and it sickens him permanently; the argument about it with FitzRoy nearly puts him off the ship for good, and neither man gives way. He is twenty-three years old and nine weeks out of Plymouth.
stops.quote: Delight itself, however, is a weak term to express the feelings of a naturalist who, for the first time, has been wandering by himself in a Brazilian forest.
stops.quote_source: Darwin, Journal of Researches, 2nd ed. (1845), Ch. II
suggested_refs: The Atlantic forest behind Salvador as Darwin walked it in February 1832
sources: Darwin, Journal of Researches, 2nd ed. (1845), Ch. II

stops.name: Rio de Janeiro, Botafogo: the cottage under the mountain
stops.date_confidence: attested for the arrival; the shore residence runs to July 1832
stops.campa: While the Beagle sails back north to re-check its longitudes, Darwin takes a cottage on Botafogo Bay and stays three months ashore, collecting insects and flatworms in quantity and riding inland to see the plantations. Through the wall of a neighbouring house he hears slaves being punished, and sets down that he could do nothing about it. He leaves Brazil with crates of insects nobody in Europe has described and a settled hatred of the institution that runs the country he collected them in.
suggested_refs: Darwin's rented cottage on Botafogo Bay, April to July 1832
sources: Darwin, Journal of Researches, 2nd ed. (1845), Ch. II

segments.name: The Plata and the Bone Beds of Punta Alta

stops.name: Montevideo: the landing party
stops.date_confidence: attested; the place is corrected from the pool, which put this landing at Buenos Aires. The Buenos Aires incident is a separate affair, the Beagle being fired on by a guard ship around 31 July 1832
stops.campa: The Beagle makes Montevideo its base on the South Atlantic and finds the town in the middle of a mutiny. The officials and the British consul ask FitzRoy for help; the garrison is held by Black troops loyal to Lavalleja. Armed seamen and marines go ashore, Darwin among them with a pistol, and hold the fort until the business subsides. A government here can be a week old, and the roads outside the town belong to whoever has the horses. He will spend more of the next two years in this region than anywhere else on earth.
suggested_refs: The fort at Montevideo, held by the Beagle's landing party on 5 August 1832
sources: Darwin, Journal of Researches, 2nd ed. (1845), Chs. III-IV

stops.name: Punta Alta: the cliff of shells and bones
stops.date_confidence: attested, from Darwin's diary as cited in the Beagle voyage article
stops.campa: A few miles from the frontier post at Bahia Blanca, Darwin and FitzRoy land at a low bluff of gravel and hardened shell standing over the beach. Teeth and bones stand out of the conglomerate. He works at it with a pickaxe through the afternoon and gets out the head of a huge animal he cannot name, and over the following weeks he keeps coming back to the same wall of rock. The shells packed into it belong to species still alive in the bay in front of him. Whatever these enormous creatures were, they died recently, and the sea beside them did not change when they went.
stops.quote: First, parts of three heads and other bones of the Megatherium, the huge dimensions of which are expressed by its name.
stops.quote_source: Darwin, Journal of Researches, 2nd ed. (1845), Ch. V
suggested_refs: The Punta Alta bluff at Bahia Blanca, source of Darwin's first fossil quadrupeds
sources: Wikipedia, 'Second voyage of HMS Beagle', citing Darwin's diary
Darwin, Journal of Researches, 2nd ed. (1845), Ch. V

stops.name: Punta Alta: the Megatherium
stops.date_confidence: attested; the pool's fossil list for this site is corrected, since the Toxodon skull came later from Mercedes and 'Hoplophorus' is not supportable, leaving ground sloth material and glyptodont armour
stops.campa: Back at the bluff in October he lifts out a skull he can put a name to: Megatherium, the giant ground sloth, known in Europe from one mounted skeleton in Madrid. Around it come the armour plates of a glyptodont and the bones of other giants, several kinds of extinct quadruped inside a few yards of the same rock. He crates them for England. The country around him still carries sloths and armadillos of the same families, alive and a fraction of the size, feeding on the ground the giants came out of. Why the big kinds went and the small ones stayed is the question he ships home with the bones.
stops.quote: the gigantic quadrupeds, more different from those of the present day than the oldest of the tertiary quadrupeds of Europe, lived whilst the sea was peopled with most of its present inhabitants
stops.quote_source: Darwin, Journal of Researches, 2nd ed. (1845), Ch. V
suggested_refs: Owen's later description of the Punta Alta ground sloths in Fossil Mammalia

segments.name: Tierra del Fuego, and the Three Who Went Home

stops.name: Good Success Bay: the first Fuegians
stops.date_confidence: the date of the first Fuegian landfall is attested; the coordinate for Bahia Buen Suceso is my own geolocation from the place name, since the pool carries only a rounded point out in open water
stops.campa: The ship anchors in a bay near the Atlantic mouth of the strait, and Fuegians come down to the shore, painted, tall, shouting and gesturing at the boat. Darwin goes ashore and meets them face to face in the wind. He has been living for a year aboard with three Fuegians in English clothes who speak English, take tea, and are being carried home to found a mission. Standing between the two facts he cannot make them meet, and what he writes about the distance between savage and civilized man he leaves standing in the book twelve years later.
stops.quote: I could not have believed how wide was the difference between savage and civilized man: it is greater than between a wild and domesticated animal.
stops.quote_source: Darwin, Journal of Researches, 2nd ed. (1845), Ch. X
suggested_refs: Bahia Buen Suceso, landfall of 18 December 1832
sources: Darwin, Journal of Researches, 2nd ed. (1845), Ch. X

stops.name: Wulaia Bay, Isla Navarino: the mission put ashore
stops.date_confidence: attested; the coordinate is corrected from the pool's -54.9333 / -67.65, which lies out in the Beagle Channel some 40 km east of the bay
stops.campa: In a sheltered bay on the western shore of Navarino, FitzRoy lands the three he took to England, and the missionary Richard Matthews with them: crockery, wine glasses, fine linen, a chest of tools, and gardens dug and planted in the peat. Jemmy Button, York Minster and Fuegia Basket are home. Yamana canoes gather along the shore to watch. Within nine days most of the goods have gone and Matthews is taken back aboard; the mission does not last a fortnight. The three are left standing on the beach as the boats pull away.
stops.quote: The language of these people, according to our notions, scarcely deserves to be called articulate.
stops.quote_source: Darwin, Journal of Researches, 2nd ed. (1845), Ch. X
suggested_refs: The mission gardens dug at Wulaia Bay in January 1833
sources: Darwin, Journal of Researches, 2nd ed. (1845), Ch. X

stops.name: Beagle Channel: the beryl-blue glaciers
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: Rowing west through the channel that carries the ship's name, the party comes under cliffs of ice that run down through the beech forest to the water's edge. A mass breaks off one of them and the wave it raises nearly carries the boats off the shingle; Darwin runs and hauls them clear, saving the party's only means of getting home. He is twenty-three and has never seen a glacier. What he sets down is the colour, and the fact that ice comes to the sea here at the latitude that in the north would give him England.
stops.quote: It is scarcely possible to imagine anything more beautiful than the beryl-like blue of these glaciers.
stops.quote_source: Darwin, Beagle diary, 29 January 1833, as quoted in Wikipedia, 'Beagle Channel'
suggested_refs: The tidewater glaciers of the northwest arm of the Beagle Channel
sources: Darwin, Journal of Researches, 2nd ed. (1845), Chs. X-XI

stops.name: Port Louis, Falkland Islands: the fox on treeless ground
stops.date_confidence: contested: the chronology lens gives February 1833, the geography lens and the Port Louis article give March and April 1833; March is used and the conflict is left standing
stops.campa: Britain has retaken the islands weeks before the Beagle anchors in Berkeley Sound, and the settlement at Port Louis is held together by an Irishman keeping order among gauchos and sealers. Darwin rides over ground with not one tree on it, puzzles at the stone runs, and gives his attention to the warrah, a wolf-like fox found on these islands and on no other land, tame enough to be knifed by a man holding meat in his other hand. He writes down that it will shortly be extinct. He is right; it is gone within forty years.
stops.quote: As far as I am aware, there is no other instance in any part of the world, of so small a mass of broken land, distant from a continent, possessing so large an aboriginal quadruped peculiar to itself.
stops.quote_source: Darwin, Journal of Researches, 2nd ed. (1845), Ch. IX
suggested_refs: The warrah, the Falkland Islands fox, extinct by 1876
sources: Darwin, Journal of Researches, 2nd ed. (1845), Ch. IX

stops.name: Maldonado: ten weeks on the Banda Oriental
stops.date_confidence: the stay of roughly late April to mid-July 1833 is attested; the exact day of arrival is not fixed in the reachable sources and is inferred
stops.campa: Put ashore on the Uruguayan coast while the ship surveys, Darwin takes lodgings in a small port and stays ten weeks, the longest he has been still since England. He hires two men, buys a horse, and rides out over the grass country collecting birds, mammals and reptiles until he has a nearly complete set of the animals of the district. Here he first watches the common rhea at close range, and hears the country talk of a second, smaller ostrich living further south, which he does not see and does not yet go out looking for.
suggested_refs: Darwin's Maldonado collection, a near-complete fauna of one district
sources: Darwin, Journal of Researches, 2nd ed. (1845), Ch. V

stops.name: Carmen de Patagones: the long ride north begins
stops.date_confidence: attested for the start of the overland journey; the town stay runs from about 3 August 1833
stops.campa: At the Patagonian frontier town on the Rio Negro he gathers a party of gauchos and sets out overland for Buenos Aires, six hundred miles across country in the middle of a war. He rides as they ride, eats meat and nothing else for days at a time, sleeps on his saddle. They teach him the bolas, with which he throws down his own horse at the first attempt, and they tell him about the avestruz petise, a smaller and darker ostrich of the south that keeps to the country the common one leaves alone. From here on he asks after it at every posta.
stops.quote: a man on horseback having thrown his lazo round the horns of a beast, can drag it any where he chooses
stops.quote_source: Darwin, Journal of Researches, 2nd ed. (1845), Ch. VI
suggested_refs: The posta system of the Rio Negro frontier, Darwin's route north in August 1833
sources: Darwin, Journal of Researches, 2nd ed. (1845), Ch. VI

stops.name: Rio Colorado: the camp of General Rosas
stops.date_confidence: attested for the meeting; the pin is inherited unchanged from juan_manuel_de_rosas.journey.json, whose own file records that its coordinate is a correction toward Pedro Luro on the river. This pool's geography lens gave -39.0167 / -64.0833 instead
stops.campa: The army of the desert is camped on the river, and to go north Darwin needs a paper from the man commanding it. Juan Manuel de Rosas receives him, talks with him, and grants the passport. Darwin sets down what he sees: a perfect horseman, grave in conversation, dressed and speaking exactly as his gauchos do, holding an unbounded power over them. He also sets down what the camp tells him without embarrassment, that the Indian men taken are killed, that the women above a certain age are killed, and that the children are given away. The passport carries him through the lines.
stops.quote: Every one here is fully convinced that this is the most just war, because it is against barbarians
stops.quote_source: Darwin, Journal of Researches, 2nd ed. (1845), Ch. VI
suggested_refs: The passport of safe conduct issued to Darwin by Rosas at the Colorado camp
sources: Darwin, Journal of Researches, 2nd ed. (1845), Chs. IV and VI

stops.name: Punta Alta: the strata read a second time
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: A year after the first digging he is back at the bluff, no longer chasing bones but reading the rock they sit in, working out which bed lies over which and what the shells in each one mean. Days later, a little inland, he gets out a skeleton lying with its bones still in the order the animal died in, undisturbed, carried there by no flood. The country made these creatures and the country buried them where they fell. The catastrophe that was supposed to have swept them away is not in the ground.
stops.quote: It is a remarkable circumstance that so many different species should be found together; and it proves how numerous in kind the ancient inhabitants of this country must have been.
stops.quote_source: Darwin, Journal of Researches, 2nd ed. (1845), Ch. V
suggested_refs: The articulated skeleton found near Bahia Blanca on 1 September 1833
sources: Darwin, Journal of Researches, 2nd ed. (1845), Ch. V

stops.name: Guardia del Monte: the most just of all wars
stops.date_confidence: the passage through the Guardia on the last leg into Buenos Aires is attested, the day is inferred. The coordinate is contested: the geography lens gives this point, the quotes lens locates the Guardia at roughly -35.43 / -58.81; the conflict is not resolved here
stops.campa: At the frontier post on the last stage into Buenos Aires he changes horses among soldiers and settlers who talk of nothing but the campaign. Everyone is for Rosas. The war is described to him in one phrase that every man at the post uses, and he copies it down in their words rather than in his own. He has just ridden through the country it is being fought in and eaten in the camp that is fighting it, kept alive night after night on the road by the hospitality of the same men who use the phrase.
stops.quote: I never saw anything like the enthusiasm for Rosas, and for the success of the 'most just of all wars, because against barbarians'
stops.quote_source: Darwin, Journal of Researches, 2nd ed. (1845), Ch. VI
suggested_refs: The frontier postas between the Guardia and Buenos Aires, ridden by Darwin in 1833
sources: Darwin, Journal of Researches, 2nd ed. (1845), Ch. VI, Wikisource and Gutenberg #944 lines 4519-4522

stops.name: Buenos Aires: the city in a revolution
stops.date_confidence: the city stay of August and September 1833 is attested; the day is inferred, and the pin is the canonical Buenos Aires coordinate already carried by the existing files
stops.campa: He comes into the city off the plain, filthy from the road, and is nearly turned back at the edge of it by rebels holding the approaches; a letter and a name get him through. Buenos Aires is in one of its revolutions, the port shut and the suburbs in the hands of the Restorer's party. Darwin lodges here between excursions and writes out how Rosas rose: elected governor and refusing the office unless the assembly conferred extraordinary powers along with it. In print he sets down that a man who takes power on those terms will end as a dictator.
stops.quote: A year ago he was elected governor, but he refused it, unless the Sala would also confer on him extraordinary powers.
stops.quote_source: Darwin, Journal of Researches, 2nd ed. (1845), Ch. VII
suggested_refs: The 1833 Restorer revolution at Buenos Aires, seen from Darwin's lodgings
sources: Darwin, Journal of Researches, 2nd ed. (1845), Chs. V and VII

stops.name: Parana bluffs near Santa Fe: the tooth of a horse
stops.date_confidence: attested to the month of October 1833; the day is the one carried by the chronology lens for the Carcarana and Parana finds
stops.campa: Riding north along the great river he works the cliffs where the water has cut into the plain, and takes out of them an enormous gnawing tooth, mastodon bones, and the tooth of a horse. The horse stops him. There were no horses in America when the Spaniards came; the Spaniards brought them, and the herds that now cover the pampas descend from strays. Yet a horse lived here and died here long before any of that, and then the whole kind went out of a continent that plainly suited it. Nothing in the country changed to account for it.
suggested_refs: The fossil horse tooth from the Parana bluffs, described later by Owen as Equus curvidens
sources: Darwin, Journal of Researches, 2nd ed. (1845), Ch. VIII

stops.name: Mercedes: a head bought for two shillings
stops.date_confidence: the Beagle voyage article puts the purchase on the day after 25 November, hence the 26th. The country is contested: the chronology lens says Mercedes in Argentina, the Toxodon article puts the type skull at Mercedes in Uruguay, whose coordinate is used here and is my own geolocation
stops.campa: Word reaches him of giant bones turned up near the town, so he rides to a house nearby and buys a skull from the people who dug it out, paying about two shillings for a head that had been quite perfect when found, before children knocked the teeth out of it for sport. Another skull from the same neighbourhood, bought about the same time for eighteen pence, will be described in London as Toxodon: an animal with the teeth of a rodent, the bulk of an elephant, the habits of a manatee, and no living order to be put into. The bones of the country are for sale at the roadside.
suggested_refs: The Toxodon platensis type skull, bought at Mercedes in November 1833

segments.name: Patagonia: the Guanaco and the Lesser Rhea

stops.name: Port Desire: a guanaco for Christmas
stops.date_confidence: attested; the ship put in on 23 December and the guanaco was shot the following day, which the pool's chronology lens had collapsed into one date
stops.campa: The ship puts into the old Spanish harbour on the Patagonian coast two days before Christmas, and the next morning Darwin goes up onto the shingle plain with a gun and shoots a guanaco of two hundred pounds, which gives the whole company its Christmas dinner. The plains behind the harbour are gravel, dry and nearly featureless, and they carry guanaco herds, foxes, and a low growth of thorn. He notes that the same few kinds of plant and animal run on unchanged for hundreds of miles in every direction he can see.
suggested_refs: The Patagonian shingle terraces behind Puerto Deseado

stops.name: Port Desire: the bird eaten before it is named
stops.date_confidence: the month is attested, the day is unknown and defaults to 01. Who fired is contested: the geography lens says Darwin, the rhea article says the ship's artist Conrad Martens, whose account is followed here
stops.campa: Conrad Martens, the ship's artist, shoots a small ostrich near the anchorage and it is plucked, cooked and served. The mess is well into the dish before Darwin, looking at what is left on it, understands that this is not a half-grown common rhea but the petise the gauchos described to him on the Rio Negro road, and that he has eaten most of the specimen he crossed Patagonia to find. He saves the head, the neck, the legs, one wing and a quantity of feathers off the table, packs them, and sends them to Henslow at Cambridge.
suggested_refs: The salvaged Port Desire rhea, sent to Henslow and described by Gould in 1837

stops.name: Port St Julian: bones he takes for a mastodon
stops.date_confidence: contested: the Beagle voyage article gives 9 January 1834, the Macrauchenia article gives 9 February 1834 for the same collection; January is used and the conflict stands
stops.campa: In the raised gravel terraces above a harbour where Magellan hanged a mutineer three hundred years earlier, Darwin digs out pieces of spine and a hind leg of something very large and guesses at a mastodon. He is wrong, and will not learn how wrong for three years. Richard Owen names it Macrauchenia, a long-necked beast built on the plan of a camel and belonging to no family now alive anywhere on earth. It lay in a terrace the sea had left behind, well above the present tide, in a country whose one large living mammal is the guanaco.
suggested_refs: Macrauchenia patachonica, named by Owen in 1837 from the Port St Julian bones

stops.name: Monte Darwin: a mountain given his name
stops.date_confidence: attested; the pool had this at reconstruction and undated, and it is upgraded, FitzRoy having named the peak for Darwin's twenty-fifth birthday
stops.campa: On his twenty-fifth birthday, with the ship working among the Fuegian channels, FitzRoy puts Darwin's name on the highest peak in sight, a snow mountain of eight thousand feet standing over the glaciers of the range. The naming is a captain's courtesy to a young man with no rank and no salary who has been aboard two years and has crates of Patagonian bones in the hold. The peak keeps the name on every chart made since, and so does the whole cordillera of ice behind it.
suggested_refs: Monte Darwin and the Cordillera Darwin, Isla Grande de Tierra del Fuego

stops.name: Wulaia Bay: Jemmy Button a year on
stops.date_confidence: attested; coordinate corrected as at the January 1833 stop
stops.campa: The Beagle comes back to the bay expecting a mission and finds nothing standing. A canoe puts out with a thin, naked, long-haired man in it whom nobody recognises until he speaks English. Jemmy Button has lost or given away everything he was left with, has a wife beside him, and has no wish at all to return to England. He comes aboard, dines with the officers, handles knife and fork correctly, sends presents ashore to his family, and goes back down into his canoe. The Beagle leaves the bay and does not come back to it.
suggested_refs: Orundellico, called Jemmy Button, c.1815 to 1864

stops.name: Santa Cruz River: boats hauled toward the Andes
stops.date_confidence: attested; corrected from the pool's 18 April, the Beagle voyage article giving the nineteenth for the start of the expedition
stops.campa: Twenty-five men in three whaleboats drag their own craft up a fast river against the current, walking the banks on a tow rope, for three weeks and two hundred miles, until the Andes stand in sight and the provisions will not stretch to reaching them. They turn and run down in three days. What Darwin takes out of it is the plain itself: gravel laid flat over old lava, terrace above terrace like the floors of a sea that has drained away, the same low thorn and the same guanaco herds the whole distance, and a condor over the cliffs at every camp.
stops.quote: The complete similarity of the productions throughout Patagonia is one of its most striking characters.
stops.quote_source: Darwin, Journal of Researches, 2nd ed. (1845), Ch. IX
suggested_refs: The Santa Cruz river terraces and their basalt sheets
sources: Darwin, Journal of Researches, 2nd ed. (1845), Chs. IX-X

segments.name: The Pacific Side: Land That Rises

stops.name: San Carlos de Chiloe: rain, forest, and a mountain on fire
stops.date_confidence: attested for the arrival; the island work runs intermittently to November 1834
stops.campa: The ship rounds into the Pacific and comes to an island of continuous rain, where the forest grows down to the tide line and the people live on potatoes and shellfish and settle their debts in planks. Darwin rides its length in the wet. From the beach at midnight in January he watches Osorno across the water throwing out incandescent matter, and learns afterwards that two other volcanoes hundreds of miles away went off in the same hours. The western edge of the continent is one machine, and it is working while he stands there.
suggested_refs: The January 1835 eruption of Osorno, seen from Chiloe
sources: Darwin, Journal of Researches, 2nd ed. (1845), Chs. XIII-XIV

stops.name: Valparaiso: the shore base
stops.date_confidence: attested for the arrival; the port serves as his base intermittently to April 1835
stops.campa: The port becomes his base for ten months, a town of English merchants and Chilean muleteers where he can leave his cases and go inland. He rides up into the cordillera and comes back with sea shells picked off ground where nothing now lives. He also spends a month flat on his back in a rented house after drinking bad wine at a mine, nursed by a schoolfellow from Shrewsbury who happens to be trading here. It is the first of the illnesses that will keep him indoors for the rest of his life, and nobody then or since has named it.
suggested_refs: Richard Corfield's house at Valparaiso, where Darwin lay ill in the winter of 1834
sources: Darwin, Journal of Researches, 2nd ed. (1845), Chs. XII and XV

stops.name: Valdivia: the ground moves
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: He is lying down in a wood near the town when the earthquake comes, and it runs two minutes. He cannot stand up; the ground moves like a thin crust over a fluid, and the trees whip against each other. The town is built of wood and does not fall, but every soul in it is out in the street. Darwin writes that a bad earthquake destroys at once the oldest associations a man has, that the world moving under the feet gives an insecurity nothing else can produce. He has been reading Lyell for three years. He is now standing on the evidence.
suggested_refs: The 20 February 1835 Concepcion earthquake, felt at Valdivia
sources: Darwin, Journal of Researches, 2nd ed. (1845), Ch. XIV

stops.name: Concepcion and Talcahuano: mussel beds nine feet up
stops.date_confidence: attested for the visit of 4 to 7 March 1835
stops.campa: Two weeks after the shock the Beagle reaches the ruined city. Every building is down, the cathedral split open, the port swept by three great waves that carried a schooner into the middle of the town. Darwin walks the shore with FitzRoy and measures the mussels: beds of dead shells still rooted to the rock, standing feet above the line where the living ones now stop. The land has been lifted in one afternoon by the force that has been lifting it all along. The Andes are built this way, a few feet at a time.
suggested_refs: The raised mussel beds at Talcahuano, measured in March 1835
sources: Darwin, Journal of Researches, 2nd ed. (1845), Ch. XIV

stops.name: Portillo Pass: sea shells at twelve thousand feet
stops.date_confidence: attested for the start of the Andes crossing, which runs to about 10 April 1835
stops.campa: He crosses the Andes by mule through a pass over twelve thousand feet, and finds marine shells in the rock near the top and, on the way up, a stand of petrified trees standing upright where they grew, set in sandstone laid down under the sea. The trees grew in open air; the sea then covered them; then the whole mass was pushed into the sky. He writes home that he can read the continent now as a slow rising, and that this is what makes the bone beds of the pampas intelligible. Nothing had to be destroyed. It only had to move.
suggested_refs: The petrified Araucaria stumps of the Uspallata range, found on the 1835 crossing
sources: Darwin, Journal of Researches, 2nd ed. (1845), Ch. XV

segments.name: Galapagos, and the Long Way Home

stops.name: San Cristobal, Galapagos: the black islands
stops.date_confidence: the ship reached the archipelago on 15 September 1835 and lay off Chatham from the 16th; the 17th is Darwin's own first landing and is the date used here
stops.campa: The Beagle raises the archipelago on the fifteenth of September and anchors off Chatham Island; Darwin lands two days later on black broken lava under a sun that makes the rock too hot to stand on. He finds giant tortoises walking worn paths to the springs, lizards feeding in the surf, and birds so unused to men that he knocks one off a branch with his hat. He has been working South America for three and a half years and has a hold full of it. The whole of his time in the archipelago will come to five weeks.
suggested_refs: Chatham Island, now San Cristobal, first Galapagos landfall
sources: Darwin, Journal of Researches, 2nd ed. (1845), Ch. XVII

stops.name: Floreana: what the vice-governor says about the shells
stops.date_confidence: attested for the visit of 24 to 27 September 1835
stops.campa: The Englishman governing the small penal settlement remarks over dinner that the tortoises differ from island to island, and that he can tell at sight which island any one of them came from by the shape of its shell. Darwin hears it, writes it down, and does not act on it. He is collecting birds without noting which island each came off, on the reasonable assumption that islands within sight of one another, of the same rock and the same climate, will hold the same animals. The correction will cost him a year of work in London.
suggested_refs: Nicholas Lawson, vice-governor at Charles Island, and his remark on the tortoise shells
sources: Darwin, Journal of Researches, 2nd ed. (1845), Ch. XVII

stops.name: Santiago Island, Galapagos: nine days ashore
stops.date_confidence: attested for the camp of 8 to 17 October 1835
stops.campa: He camps for nine days with his servant and a party of Spaniards salting fish, and collects harder here than anywhere else in the group: plants, lizards, tortoises, and the small dull finches whose beaks run from a thick crushing bill at one end of the series to a warbler's point at the other. He weighs the tortoises' bladders for drinkable water and rides on their backs. The labels he writes say the archipelago, not the island. When John Gould in London sorts the finches into species, the missing labels have to be rebuilt from FitzRoy's collection and from memory.
suggested_refs: Darwin's finch specimens and the relabelling from FitzRoy's parallel collection
sources: Darwin, Journal of Researches, 2nd ed. (1845), Ch. XVII

stops.name: Sydney: two acts of creation, and a line drawn through them
stops.date_confidence: attested for the stay of 12 to 30 January 1836
stops.campa: Riding inland toward Bathurst he lies down by a pool in the heat and watches a platypus at work, and in the dry grass an ant-lion digging its pit exactly as the European kind digs it. A disbeliever in everything beyond his own reason, he writes in his diary, might well exclaim that surely two distinct Creators must have been at work here. Then he thinks about the ant-lion, one contrivance made twice in two separated worlds, and he puts a line through the sentence.
suggested_refs: The Sydney diary entry of January 1836 and its struck-out passage on two Creators
sources: Darwin, Journal of Researches, 2nd ed. (1845), Ch. XIX

stops.name: Cocos (Keeling): the atoll he had already worked out
stops.date_confidence: attested for the stay of 1 to 12 April 1836
stops.campa: He walks a ring of coral in the Indian Ocean, sounds the outer slope, and finds living coral only in the top few fathoms with dead rock below it going down past the reach of the line. The theory is already written; he had it before he ever saw a reef, out of the raised beaches of Chile. If the sea floor sinks as slowly as the Andes rise, the coral builds upward as fast as its foundation goes down, and the ring left at the surface is the outline of a drowned island. The ocean is doing in reverse what he watched Chile do in one afternoon.
suggested_refs: The subsidence theory of atoll formation, tested at Keeling in 1836
sources: Darwin, Journal of Researches, 2nd ed. (1845), Ch. XX

stops.name: Falmouth: ashore in the dark
stops.date_confidence: attested
stops.campa: The Beagle comes in to Falmouth in a gale at night after four years, nine months and five days, and Darwin does not wait for the morning or for the ship to be paid off. He goes ashore at once, takes the mail coach, and travels two days across England to walk into his father's house at Shrewsbury in time for breakfast, having told nobody he was coming. He is twenty-seven. Behind him in the hold are thousands of specimens, the notebooks, and the bones out of the cliff at Punta Alta, which have not yet been looked at by anyone who can name them.
suggested_refs: The Beagle's return to Falmouth, 2 October 1836
sources: Darwin, Journal of Researches, 2nd ed. (1845), Ch. XXI

segments.name: London, Down House, and What the Bones Meant

stops.name: London, Zoological Society: the lesser rhea gets a name
stops.date_confidence: the year is attested; the month and day of the meeting are not fixed in the reachable sources and default to 01
stops.campa: The salvaged head, neck and legs from the dinner at Port Desire are laid before the Zoological Society, and John Gould describes them as new to science and names the bird Rhea darwinii. Darwin reads a paper at the same meeting on the eggs of the two rheas and on where each of them lives, which is the part that concerns him. The two are distinct, they are close kin, and their ranges meet and overlap in Patagonia rather than being held apart by anything a map would show. One does not become the other by crossing a river.
suggested_refs: Gould's 1837 description of Rhea darwinii, later synonymised with Rhea pennata

stops.name: London: Owen takes the bones apart
stops.date_confidence: the Fossil Mammalia was issued in numbers from 1838 to 1840 rather than published on one day, the whole Zoology running to October 1843; the opening year is used and the month defaults to 01
stops.campa: Richard Owen works through the Punta Alta and Patagonian fossils and publishes them in numbers as the first part of the Zoology of the Voyage of H.M.S. Beagle. The giants come out of the crates carrying names: Megatherium, Scelidotherium, Mylodon darwinii, Macrauchenia, Toxodon. What the anatomy shows is that most of them are outsized relatives of animals still walking about the same country, sloths, armadillos, llamas. Extinct kinds and living kinds stand in the same place on the same continent, one after the other, in the same order everywhere he dug.
stops.quote: the Scelidotherium, also an allied animal, of which I obtained a nearly perfect skeleton. It must have been as large as a rhinoceros
stops.quote_source: Darwin, Journal of Researches, 2nd ed. (1845), Ch. V
suggested_refs: Owen, Fossil Mammalia, Part 1 of the Zoology of the Voyage of H.M.S. Beagle, 1838-1840
sources: en.wikipedia.org, 'Zoology of the Voyage of H.M.S. Beagle'

stops.name: London: the Journal of Researches
stops.date_confidence: attested for the separate Colburn issue; the text had appeared in May 1839 as the third volume of FitzRoy's Narrative
stops.campa: His account of the voyage appears as the third volume of FitzRoy's Narrative, is read more than the other two, and is issued on its own by Colburn in August. It sells for the rest of the century. The chapters that carry it are not the five weeks in the Galapagos, which take one: they are Bahia Blanca and the bones, the ride across the pampas on Rosas's passport, Tierra del Fuego and Jemmy Button, and the guanaco and the two ostriches of Patagonia. John Murray buys the copyright in 1845 for a hundred and fifty pounds and reissues it revised.
suggested_refs: The 1845 Murray second edition, the text later retitled The Voyage of the Beagle in 1905

stops.name: Down House, Kent: twenty years with the crates
stops.date_confidence: the residence from 1842 to 1882 is attested; the household moved in the autumn of 1842 and the month here is inferred
stops.campa: He buys a plain house in a village sixteen miles out of London and hardly leaves it again for forty years. The specimens are worked through, handed to specialists, argued over and set aside; the notebooks fill; the illnesses arrive and stay. A gravel path is laid around the garden and he walks it every day, counting the circuits with flints kicked off a pile. On the Origin of Species is published in 1859, twenty-three years after Falmouth, and its argument runs on evidence he took out of the ground at Punta Alta before he was twenty-four.
suggested_refs: The Sandwalk at Down House, paced daily from 1846
sources: Browne, Charles Darwin: The Power of Place (2002)
Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1859)

stops.name: Westminster Abbey: the burial he did not ask for
stops.date_confidence: attested for the funeral; he died at Down House on 19 April 1882
stops.campa: He dies at Down House on the nineteenth of April and expects the churchyard at Downe, where two of his children lie. His scientific colleagues and twenty members of parliament petition otherwise, and the family gives way. He is carried into the Abbey and buried in the north aisle of the nave, close by the monument to Isaac Newton, with the president of the Royal Society among the pallbearers. Twenty-three years after the Origin, the established church of England buries its author a few paces from Newton, among the mathematicians.
suggested_refs: The grave in the north aisle of the nave, Westminster Abbey

stops.name: Punta Alta: the museum on the bone ground
stops.date_confidence: no founding date is given in the reachable source, which names the institution without dating it; the year here is a placeholder and should be replaced when a date is found
stops.campa: The naval town grown up beside the gravel bluff keeps a municipal natural sciences museum and names it for him, Carlos Darwin, in the Spanish of the country whose frontier war he rode through with a passport in his pocket. The cliff he dug is a few minutes away down the coast. What came out of it, the ground sloths and the armour plates and the small extinct rodents of Monte Hermoso, went to England in crates and stayed there. Only the name comes back to the ground it was made on.
suggested_refs: Museo Municipal de Ciencias Naturales Carlos Darwin, Punta Alta
